subject: Critical Thinking
title: Misinformation vs. Disinformation vs. Malinformation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Misinformation vs. Disinformation vs. Malinformation.

hook.text: Your aunt shares a fake cure on Facebook. A state actor plants fake election data.

buildup.text: Misinformation: false, shared without intent to harm. Disinformation: false, shared deliberately to deceive.

discovery.text: The distinction matters because the solutions differ: education for misinformation, detection for disinformation.

twist.text: Most misinformation is spread by ordinary people who believe it. They're victims of disinformation, not perpetrators.

climax.text: Before sharing anything: Is it true? Is the source reliable? Could it cause harm? These three seconds save reputations.

punchline.text: False & intentional is disinformation. False & innocent is misinformation.

quiz.question: What distinguishes disinformation from misinformation?
options: Disinformation is deliberately false; misinformation is unintentionally false

details.summary: Misinformation is false content shared without harmful intent, disinformation is deliberately fabricated to deceive, and malinformation is true content shared to cause harm. Distinguishing these three categories is essential for calibrating your response.
details.whyItMatters: Different types of information disorder require different responses. Correcting honest mistakes differs from countering deliberate deception or weaponized truth.
takeaways: Misinformation is unintentional; disinformation is deliberate
Malinformation uses real facts weaponized for harmful purposes
Intent matters for response strategy even when the content is identical

faq.question: Can you give a clear example of each type of information disorder?
faq.answer: Misinformation: sharing a satire article believing it is real news. Disinformation: a state actor creating a fake news site to influence an election. Malinformation: leaking someone's private medical records to discredit them. All cause harm but through different mechanisms.

faq.question: Why is it important to know the intent behind false information?
faq.answer: Intent determines the appropriate response. Misinformation can often be corrected with gentle factual correction. Disinformation requires exposing the source and their motives. Malinformation raises ethical questions about privacy and the weaponization of truth.
